title: Lumber Ports of the California Coast
subtitle: Doghole chutes to deepwater harbors, c.1850–1940 — with the railroads that fed them
abstract: Every documented lumber shipping point on the California coast, from chute-only dogholes where two-masted schooners moored under a cliff to the deepwater mills of Humboldt Bay — with the loading technology (trough chute, wire chute, pier), the operating companies, the cargo streams (sawn redwood, railroad ties, tanoak bark, split stuff, cordwood, Douglas fir, farm produce), the logging railroads that reached tidewater, and the lighthouses this deadly trade built. Pin size shows the four-tier port classification; filters cut by class, cargo, and company; era buttons snap the timeline to the trade's four periods. The Sonoma-Mendocino core follows the NRHP Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape inventory (57 ports, draft 2021) with dates keyed to the U.S. Coast Pilot editions (1869, 1889, 1909); dates are circa and lag reality by their source's edition. Coordinates carry per-pin provenance (GNIS records, Coast Pilot verbal geometry, NRHP archaeology) and were validated against the inventory's own north-to-south ordering and Davidson's stated inter-port distances. COVERAGE IS ASYMMETRIC: no inventory of comparable rigor exists for Humboldt, Del Norte, or the coast south of the Golden Gate; those zones are assembled from county histories, NPS studies, and the Coast Pilots, and are necessarily less complete. Six documented ports have no confirmed location and are deliberately not pinned: Monroe, Devilbliss, the Unnamed Landing near Uncle Abe's, Uncle Abe's, Buster's, and Scott's (the last two may be one site). The sailing lumber fleet these ports loaded survives in exactly one vessel: the schooner C.A. Thayer (Bendixsen yard, Fairhaven, 1895 — search 'thayer' to follow her thread), preserved at San Francisco's Hyde Street Pier.
legend_note: Pin size = port class (doghole → deepwater). Dashed/hollow pins are approximate. Six documented ports with unknown locations are listed in the About panel, not pinned. Dashed rail lines are reconstructed corridors between documented points, not surveyed alignments.

features.name: Needle Rock Landing
features.summary: The northernmost Mendocino doghole port, half-way between Bear Harbor and Shelter Cove. A wire-chute pier reputedly the highest and longest on the Mendocino coast shipped railroad ties, tanbark, and Whitethorn Valley shingles from the 1890s; a 3-mile railway (1890, Stetson) linked mill and landing. Chute operated until about 1930, making it one of the longest-lived Lost Coast landings.

small pier carrying the wire chute (MPDF); no conventional wharf

features.name: Bear Harbor Landing
features.summary: The definitive Lost Coast doghole port: split-products (above all tanbark) exported by schooner from 1874 and by steam schooner from 1890 over two successive pier-and-chute systems, fed after 1893 by the Bear Harbor & Eel River Railroad with its 2,000-ft gravity incline over the coastal ridge. The Southern Humboldt Lumber Co.'s half-million-dollar Andersonia sawmill was finished in 1905 but destroyed by the 18 April 1906 earthquake before ever cutting lumber; the port shipped its last products in 1907. 46+ vessels carried cargoes to 14 California ports over 33 years.
facts: Two successive hybrid pier+chute systems: (1) 1885 pier off Morgan Rock with trough-chute apron arm at its end (Peterson 1885 survey; Davidson 1889 describes wharf 'with an apron over fifteen feet of water'); (2) June 1890, new 300-ft pier at Cluster Cone Rocks with WIRE chute at its end ('similar to the one at Noyo Landing'), extended 100 ft in 1892 and again ~1895/1898; SF Chronicle 16 Jan 1898: wharf 250 ft through rocks, wire runs 420 ft to the vessel ~40 ft above water. Donkey engine powered the wire (a spark from the chute's donkey engine burned 400 ft of pier 8 Apr 1903). 1901 rebuild put on 1,500 ties/hour, 'fastest work ever done over a wire chute in Mendocino County' (Ukiah Dispatch 15 Nov 1901)

yes - pier (not a true wharf per NR nomination terminology); 550-600 ft after all extensions; destroyed by 14-ft 'tidal wave' 21 Nov 1899 (2 killed, incl. near-miss of company president Calvin Stewart), rebuilt 1901; burned in part 1903; destroyed again by storms Christmas 1905; partially rebuilt 1906-07

Bear Harbor Lumber Co. railway, completed June 1893: 2.0-mile cable+adhesion line from pier, with 2,000-ft incline rising 600 ft (NR nomination; North Coast Journal gives 1,900 ft at 31% grade) - gravity-balanced, rails splitting at midpoint for passing (NR says three rails; NCJ says four tracks at midpoint); extended to Moody on Indian Creek (10 mi from port), +1.5 mi 1895, +3 mi to Eel River 1898, ~18 mi of track by fall 1905 with dozens of trestles (many >300 ft) and a 200-ft tunnel; Bear Harbor & Eel River RR Co. from Sept 1896. GAUGE CONFLICT: NR narrative says standard gauge; the recorded archaeological feature (MEN-2149H) is narrow-gauge track, and a 1977 CA State Parks inventory found BOTH narrow and standard gauge rails - flag unresolved. Motive power: Shay 0-4-0 'Gypsy' No. 1 (Marschutz & Cantrell, SF); Baldwin 2-4-2T No. 2 (1898); horses along the coast leg. FATE: 1899 wave, 1903 fire, 1904 forest fire (1 mi of track + 2,900 ft of bridges), Anderson killed by falling timber Oct 28/died Nov 4 1905, Christmas 1905 storm destroyed pier, 18 Apr 1906 earthquake wrecked the Andersonia mill, log-pond dam, and track - the $500,000 mill NEVER ran; 5,000,000 ft of sawed logs abandoned in the pond; 1907 last shipment ends activity

features.name: Rockport Landing (Cottoneva Cove, Miller's Chute)
features.summary: William R. Miller landed mill machinery from the schooner David and Edward in October 1876 and built the first sawmill; the wharf-and-chute complex of 1876 cost $14,000 and was called the finest on the Mendocino coast (Palmer: 275-ft suspension span with seven cables a side). The 1889 Coast Pilot describes the mature system: a 175-yard wire suspension bridge from the north point to a 50-ft rock, a tramway across the rock, and a 45-yard chute over 15 ft of water; four principal mooring buoys; mill (25,000 ft/day) 1/3 mi up Cottoneva Creek, lumber brought by tramway, logs by steam railway; ~24 cargoes/yr; landing unused about four months after 1 December. Ownership: Miller to Cottoneva Lumber Co. 1886 (mill burned 1900); New York & Pennsylvania (Redwood) Co. c.1907 built a new mill (also burned); Cottoneva Lumber Co. reincorporated 1910 (nothing built); Finkbine-Guild Lumber Co. 1925-27 (financial disaster); Southern Redwood Co. 1928-29; Rockport Redwood Co. chartered under Dusenbury interests in the 1930s (trucking era).
facts: suspension bridge + island tramway + trough chute (15 ft water); largest 'anchorage... large in comparison with Westport, Kibesillah, Newport' (1889 CP)

features.name: Hardy Creek Landing
features.summary: Mill settlement just around the point from Rockport; the mill was part of the Cottoneva Lumber Co. of Rockport and was operated by E.T. Dusenbury, one of its owners. It had its own wharf and a railroad, and the town a large hotel; the mill burned and was never rebuilt. The 1889 Coast Pilot already names Hardy's Rock on this shore; the mill era therefore falls in the Cottoneva Lumber Co. period (c.1886-1900s) but exact years are unverified.

features.name: Union Landing (McFaul's Landing)
features.summary: Busy shipping point without a mill of its own, serving many small mills nearby (incl. the Juan Creek timber). W.P. McFaul built the first wharf, shipping six-foot railroad ties to San Pedro for the Los Angeles Railway. After W.P. Frick acquired the Big Juan Creek timber in 1920, he had a new wharf built in 1926 — the last wharf ever built on the Mendocino coast — which the Depression left barely used. A large hotel/boarding house served the wharf hands.

features.name: Westport Landing (Switzer's Chute, Beall's)
features.summary: First settled by Samuel Beal(l) (hence Beal's Landing); Fred Helmke's unfranchised 1875 chute soon washed away; James T. Rodgers built the wharf and chute in 1877 and renamed the town (Palmer 1880 says for Eastport, Maine; Wikipedia says Westport, Connecticut — unresolved). Palmer: a 375-ft wharf, 20 ft wide, with a ~200-ft suspension span, its outer end on a large rock, carrying two chutes. A new 610-ft chute with 75-ft apron (1882) let the loaded car haul the empty back. Two chutes (N and S) served three mills on Wages Creek plus DeHaven, Howard Creek and other feeders; ~65 vessels/yr, up to 85,000 ft loaded in a day; shipping suspended four months each winter, moorings lifted and overhauled. The south wharf was abandoned by 1900 and the port faded after WWI with the tie market.
facts: wharf-with-suspension-span carrying two chutes; second 610-ft chute 1882; extensive outer moorings
small landing railroad on the wharf/bluff (locomotive visible in photos); Howard Creek later ran a small rail to the Westport wharf

features.name: Kibesilah Landing (Ackermann's Landing)
features.summary: Settled in the 1860s (first business, a blacksmith shop, 1867), Kibesillah grew to 20-30 buildings with three hotels and its own newspaper, shipping posts, cordwood and tanbark (not lumber, per Palmer) over its chute. The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a very substantial 90-yard wharf continued by an apron over 20 ft of water — but by 1885 no moorings were laid and the landing was 'practically abandoned,' vessels having no demand for ties there. When Stewart, Hunter and Johnson moved the mill to Fort Bragg in 1885 the town followed — hence 'the Mother of Fort Bragg.'
facts: chute; later substantial wharf + apron (20 ft water)

features.name: Newport Landing
features.summary: 'One of the most contracted anchorages on the coast' — a cove 150 by 60 yards. The Field Brothers' mill (2 mi east on Mill Creek, Ten Mile drainage) burned 1877; brothers-in-law Calvin Stewart and James Hunter rebuilt it in 1878 (25,000 ft/day) and hauled lumber by six-horse jerk-line teams to a 260-ft gravity chute reaching 18 ft of water; a 200-ton vessel could load amid an elaborate web of six-plus moorings — no spot on the coast demanded more shiphandling skill. ~50 vessels/yr. C.R. Johnson bought in 1882, concluded the port could never grow, and moved the mill to Fort Bragg in 1885; by 1887 only posts and ties were loaded, and the landing died.
facts: single gravity/apron chute, 260 ft, to 18 ft water; extensive moorings; no wharf

features.name: Laguna Landing (Cleone Landing)
features.summary: The Dwelly brothers took timber on Laguna Creek early in 1883, built a water-powered mill and the original chute and wharf at Cleone Point, shipping their first load by July 1883; the Little Valley Lumber Co. (Barto, Jarvis, Nichols, Salsig, inc. 23 May 1885) combined this with the Mill Creek mill near Inglenook. The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a ~160-yard wharf with attached apron chute (vessel under it in 12 ft; 100-ton vessels; five moorings; mill 3 mi east at 18,000 ft/day), reported washed away in 1886 with business transferring to Fort Bragg — but rights to rebuild wharf and chute were granted in 1888, the wharf grew from 332 to ~500 ft (35 ft above the breakers; 300 ft collapsed to teredo worms Nov 1885, rebuilt), with loading wires extending to steam schooners ~200 ft offshore. A 2.5-mile wooden-strap-rail tramway ran gravity-down/horses-up through town; Union Lumber acquired all in 1901 and relaid light steel; the Laguna mill closed November 1904, ending the port.
facts: wharf + apron chute; later loading wires to offshore steam schooners

features.name: Fort Bragg Landing (Soldiers Harbor)
features.summary: The military post (est. 1857 to watch the reservation; abandoned by the mid-1860s — 'many years ago' per 1889 CP) gave its name to the cove C.R. Johnson chose after judging Newport hopeless: with Calvin Stewart and James Hunter he formed the Fort Bragg Redwood Co. (1885), moved the Kibesillah mill down, incorporated the Fort Bragg Railroad 30 April 1885 (rails up Pudding Creek; Glen Blair 1887), and built the wharf in Soldiers Harbor — incomplete July 1885, a working shipping landing in 1886, where 'steam schooners only load' (1889 CP). Union Lumber Co. formed 1891 (merging Noyo River Lumber Co.); National Steamship Co. 1901; California Western RR & Navigation Co. 1905, over the hill to Willits 1911 — after which Fort Bragg was the only coast mill with rail access to market. The pier grew to ~700 ft with three tracks and cranes; the last lumber cargo to leave the Mendocino coast by sea sailed from this pier in 1938. Mill (later Boise Cascade/Georgia-Pacific) ran until 21 June 2002.
facts: pier/wharf with cranes (steam schooners; sail on the north side); no chute

features.name: Noyo Landing (Noyo Anchorage)
features.summary: Capt. William Richardson had a mill built 3 mi up the Noyo in 1852-53 (washed out January 1854); A.W. Macpherson (& Weatherby) opened the lasting Noyo mill in 1858 (40,000 ft/day by 1880, ~120 million ft cut). Uniquely for this coast there was NO chute: lumber was lightered from a wharf inside the river mouth to vessels at two mooring buoys in the cove, small schooners filling holds in the river; ships drawing 23 ft loaded direct for foreign ports (one cargo to Valparaiso), a tug shared with Albion towing vessels out; five vessels a month in ordinary seasons and the coasting steamer every trip (1889 Coast Pilot). The mill built one of the coast's earliest railroads, hauling logs from Pudding Creek along today's Harrison Street; the company merged into Union Lumber in 1891.
facts: wharf-inside-river + lighters to moorings; no chute (Palmer explicit)

features.name: Caspar Landing (Caspar Anchorage)
features.summary: William H. Kelley & Randall built the sawmill at Caspar Creek mouth in 1861; Jacob Green Jackson bought it in 1864, incorporated the Caspar Lumber Co. in 1880, and his son-in-law Henry Krebs ran it from 1901 until closure 18 November 1955 — the longest-lived family firm on the coast. The 1889 Coast Pilot: two lumber chutes on the north bluff (11 and 18 ft of water), excellent moorings overhauled each winter, four vessels loading at once, flag signals, ~50 vessels/yr, 150 million ft shipped to date. Its railroad began 1874 as a 1.5-mi wooden-railed horse/mule tram to Jughandle Creek, got a locomotive in 1875, crossed Jughandle trestle 1884 (Caspar & Hare Creek RR), and was incorporated 1903 as the standard-gauge Caspar, South Fork & Eastern (tunnel 1904; 30 mi by 1924; Mallets from 1910; rail to 1945). Company steamships (e.g. the 1888-built Caspar) carried the cut until trucking began 1939.
facts: two trough chutes (11/18 ft water), interconnected moorings 'after the manner of Mendocino City'; later loading gear for company steamers

features.name: Mendocino Landing (Big River Landing)
features.summary: Founded on the Frolic: the Baltimore-built opium brig wrecked at Point Cabrillo 25 July 1850; Henry Meiggs's salvage agent Jerome Ford found no cargo but reported the redwood, and Meiggs's brig Ontario landed mill machinery in July 1852 (California Lumber Co.; first mill on the point 1852, second on the river flats 1853-54; reorganized after Meiggs's 1854 failure, eventually the Mendocino Lumber Co.; mill burned 17 Oct 1863, rebuilt 1864, 55,000 ft/day both sides) — the origin story verified against Thomas Layton's Frolic research. A railroad with a 64-ft stationary-engine incline linked mill to chutes. Production halted 1937; the last ship, steamer Noyo, took a deckload 24 November 1938.

features.name: Cuffey's Cove Landing
features.summary: Settled by Frank Farnier ('Portuguese Frank') and Nathaniel Smith; James Kenney's chute/landing franchise dates to 28 March 1868. features.name: Eureka (Humboldt Bay)

date.display: 1850-1940s+ (first sawmill and first lumber cargo 1850; first redwood cargo 1855; timber port for over a century)

features.summary: California's redwood metropolis: nine mills on the bay by 1854, the first redwood cargo 1855, and by 1889 'the great lumber center of this region' with enormous shipping, direct foreign trade, and eight feeder railroads (Davidson). Its notorious shifting bar bred the earliest tug-assisted bar-crossing system on the coast (c.1852) and, from 1889-91, federal jetties. John Dolbeer's donkey engine (Eureka, Aug 1881) mechanized West Coast logging from here. The NWP's completion (23 Oct 1914) turned the lumber flow from sea to rail, though steam schooners persisted into the 1920s-30s.
facts: Wharves along the Eureka waterfront - 'Vessels lie at the wharves to load lumber and produce, and rest on the mud at low-tide' (Davidson 1889); mill-side wharves on Indian/Gunther Island ('extensive saw-mill buildings and wharves,' 1889); channel to Eureka dredged by U.S. Engineers (1889). BAR SYSTEM: shifting bar with 13-25 ft; steam tug stationed on the bar from c.1852 - flag hoisted on Red Bluff, tug goes out, 'The best advice we can offer in regard to entering the bay is to wait for the tug' (Davidson 1869); pilots' flagstaff ranges on Red Bluff; lumber-laden vessels detained up to 25-31 days in bad weather (1851, 1861); can-buoy moorings outside (1869). USACE jetties: two-parallel-jetty plan in Chief of Engineers Annual Report 1877; south jetty begun 1889, north jetty 1891 (Magoon, Sloan & Shimizu 1976)
yes - multiple town and mill wharves from the 1850s

Carson et al.; 25 mi Eureka-Burnells, standard gauge, ~2,000-ft Table Bluff tunnel; to SF & Northwestern Oct 1902, NWP later); Pacific Lumber's connection at Alton (1885) and spur to Fields Landing (1884); Bucksport & Elk River RR (Dolbeer & Carson + Elk River Mill, 1885 log line, 12 mi); Eureka & Klamath River RR (inc. 1893, Vance: Samoa-Essex, Eureka by ferry); Humboldt Northern Ry (Carson, 1905, Cole's Landing north toward McKinleyville); Arcata & Mad River (see Arcata); Oregon & Eureka (Hammond, see Samoa). NWP golden spike at Cain Rock 23 Oct 1914 connected Humboldt Bay to San Francisco by rail - rail then replaced steam schooners as the main means of getting Humboldt lumber to market (Timber Heritage Assoc.; Humboldt Co. Hist. Soc.)

features.name: Samoa

date.display: 1892/1894-1940s+ (Vance mill's first lumber 1894; Hammond era 1900-1956; Louisiana-Pacific after)

features.summary: The Vance heirs' 1892-94 Samoa mill - largest in Humboldt County - became the West Coast flagship of A.B. Hammond's empire after his $1,000,000 purchase of 1 Sept 1900. Hammond shipped redwood from his own dock in his own vessels, ran the Oregon & Eureka RR up the coast to Crannell/Trinidad (into the NWP 1907), and built seven wooden steamships at Samoa during WWI. Logging lines reached Big Lagoon until fire destroyed the trestles in 1945.

features.name: Trinidad

date.display: 1850-c.1920s (gold-rush supply port 1850-50s; lumber wharf by 1869; mill-company port through the 1880s-90s; Hammond owned the waterfront until 1944; whaling pier in the early 20th c.)

features.summary: Discovered for the sea by the gold rush (Dec 1849-1850), Trinidad was the miners' landing for the Klamath diggings while 'great amounts of lumber... were shipped south to build San Francisco.' features.name: Klamath River mouth / Requa
features.summary: Not a conventional port but a genuine export point: after failed 1880s mill ventures at the treacherous Klamath bar, Bull & Dunn's 1920s cedar was bound into Davis-patent ocean rafts of several million feet, floated over the bar at flood tide and towed to Eureka for trans-shipment to Japan - the coast's most exotic solution to a barred river mouth.

features.name: Crescent City

date.display: 1853-1939 as a lumber port (town 1853; first lumber wharf/cargo 1869-70; Hobbs Wall shutdown 22 Feb 1939); harbor breakwater era 1920s+; post-1945 truck-logging revival shipped by other means

features.summary: Del Norte's only real port: a rock-strewn open roadstead that Davidson called the most dangerous regularly used on the coast, yet from the 1869 community mill venture and the 1871 arrival of Hobbs, Pomeroy (later Hobbs, Wall & Co.) it shipped spruce and redwood lumber and millions of boxes to San Francisco for seven decades. Hobbs Wall's mills, 12-mile Crescent City & Smith River RR (1890-94), wharf-spur locomotives (1903), and company steamers Del Norte, Mandalay, and Westport made it a company county until the sudden shutdown of February 1939.

Johnson); first lumber cargo left aboard schooner Fanny Jane (Capt. Peter Caughell); lighters loaded directly from the wharf as it extended. Battery Point wharf noted by Davidson 1869 ('landing is now easily effected in good weather. In southeasters the breakers wash over it'); coasting steamers anchored close in and discharged into lighters. Rail spur to the wharf (first railroad in Del Norte, Hobbs-Pomeroy 1870s); first locomotive on the new wharf track May 1903
